name: langchain
title: LangChain: The Agent Engineering Framework for AI Applications
answer: LangChain is an MIT-licensed Python framework for building AI applications, especially agents, that connect language models to tools, data and each other. It sits above model providers and below your application, offering integrations, orchestration and tracing through LangSmith. The one thing to know before adopting it is that its official documentation now centres on the hosted LangSmith platform, so teams wanting a purely local, self-managed stack should check how much of the workflow depends on that service.

sections.body: LangChain is made by LangChain, the company behind the langchain-ai organisation on GitHub, and it is an open source framework released under the MIT licence. The repository is langchain-ai/langchain, written primarily in Python, with a JavaScript and TypeScript counterpart documented separately. It first appeared in 2022 and has since grown into one of the most starred AI projects on GitHub, with 147,408 stars recorded at the time of writing and a last push on 3 October 2026. In the AI stack it occupies the orchestration layer: it does not train models and does not serve them at the lowest level, but it sits between model providers such as OpenAI, Anthropic, Google and Mistral and the application a developer is building. Its own description is the agent engineering platform, which signals that its centre of gravity has moved from simple prompt chains to agents that call tools, retrieve data and run multi-step workflows. The official documentation lives at docs.langchain.com, and the Python overview page is the entry point for the open source library.
sections.heading: What it is and where it sits in AI work

sections.body: The concrete jobs LangChain does are broad. It provides chat model and text completion integrations for many providers, including Google Gemini through ChatGoogleGenerativeAI, Fireworks, MistralAI and others, and it supports tool calling, structured output, image, audio and video input, token-level streaming, token usage reporting and logprobs. It is used for retrieval, for grounding generation in real-world information through tools such as Google's built-in search, and for agents that combine models with external functions. It is also the client side of LangSmith, the company's observability and evaluation platform, which traces model calls, supports model fallbacks in the LLM Gateway, and offers an auth proxy for enterprise deployments. Where it is strongest is in breadth of integrations and in the speed of assembling a working agent from existing parts. A developer who wants one interface across many providers, or who wants tracing and evaluation without building it, gets the most from it. Teams with a single model and a narrow, latency-critical path may find the abstraction adds more than it removes.
sections.heading: What it is used for and where it is strongest

sections.body: The learning curve is moderate and mostly practical rather than mathematical. A working knowledge of Python or TypeScript, plus comfort with APIs and asynchronous code, is enough to start, and the official site offers quickstart material, integration pages and examples for each provider. There is no requirement to understand transformer internals or training mathematics, because LangChain consumes hosted or locally served models rather than building them. The harder parts are conceptual: understanding how chains, tools, memory and agents compose, and how tracing and evaluation fit around them. The documentation is extensive but uneven, with some pages warning that an integration is based on a deprecated library, as the Google Generative AI page does, and pointing to a replacement. A beginner should expect to read several pages before a first agent works, and should treat the LangSmith material as a separate product with its own plans and permissions rather than as part of the core library.
sections.heading: How hard it is to learn and what you need first

sections.body: The ecosystem is the strongest argument for LangChain. The official site documents integrations across chat models, completion models, tools, retrievers and vector stores, with packages such as @langchain/google-genai, @langchain/fireworks and @langchain/mistralai for JavaScript and equivalents for Python. It connects to the Vercel AI SDK through LangSmithTelemetry and wrapAISDK, supports OpenTelemetry for older versions, and can be connected to an agent of choice via MCP for real-time answers, as the Fireworks page notes. LangSmith adds tracing, evaluation, a playground, an LLM Gateway with model fallbacks and credits, and an Envoy-based auth proxy for enterprise customers. Community support is large, reflected in the star count and the volume of documentation, though the site itself is the primary reference. The documentation is organised by language and by integration, which makes it navigable but also means answers are spread across many pages.
sections.heading: Ecosystem and community

sections.body: LangChain is built for both, but with different costs. For prototyping it is fast: a developer can swap providers, add tools and get tracing with little code, and the integration pages give copyable examples. For production it offers real controls, including model fallbacks that retry against backup models on rate limits or provider errors, spend policies that cap usage per organisation, workspace, API key or user, and an auth proxy that keeps provider credentials out of end users' hands. Those controls are largely delivered through LangSmith, and several require paid plans or enterprise features. The cost of the abstraction is that the framework sits in the request path, so latency and memory are affected by its layers, and the documentation does not publish benchmarks for that overhead. A team should prototype with LangChain and then measure, rather than assume the same code is optimal at scale.
sections.heading: Prototyping speed against production performance

sections.body: LangChain is a current standard rather than a legacy choice, at least by visibility and integration count. Its 147,408 GitHub stars and its use as the client for LangSmith indicate wide adoption, and the documentation covers enterprise features such as single sign-on style auth proxies, spend policies and self-hosted deployments, which suggests use in organisations rather than only in side projects. For someone choosing what to learn, it is a reasonable default for agent and retrieval work in Python or TypeScript, and familiarity with it transfers to many job descriptions. The caveat is that the field moves quickly and the framework has changed shape over time, from chains toward agents and the LangSmith platform. The facts and the site do not give user numbers, revenue or named customers, so claims about market share beyond the star count and the breadth of integrations would be speculation.
sections.heading: Industry adoption and careers

sections.body: LangChain is typically used with Python or JavaScript and TypeScript, and it is designed to sit above model providers rather than replace them. It is commonly paired with OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Mistral, Fireworks and other inference platforms, with vector databases for retrieval, and with the Vercel AI SDK on the JavaScript side, where LangSmith provides tracing through LangSmithTelemetry or wrapAISDK. It also fits beside OpenTelemetry for observability and beside LiteLLM or an internal gateway when an organisation already has one, since the auth proxy can forward to an upstream gateway. The polyglot pattern is a Python or TypeScript application using LangChain for orchestration, one or more hosted or self-hosted models behind it, and LangSmith or another observability tool alongside it. It is not a training framework and does not compete with PyTorch or TensorFlow, and it is not a serving runtime in the sense that vLLM or TensorRT are.
sections.heading: How it fits beside the others

sections.body: The clearest limits are that LangChain is an orchestration layer, so it inherits the weaknesses of the models and services beneath it, and that much of its production value now depends on LangSmith, which is a commercial product with paid plans and enterprise-only features such as the auth proxy. Some integrations are deprecated or based on deprecated libraries, as the Google Generative AI page states, which means maintenance attention is uneven across the catalogue. The documentation does not publish performance benchmarks, does not quantify adoption beyond repository stars, and does not say how much of the open source library can be used without the hosted platform. It also does not settle questions about long-term API stability or the cost of the abstraction in latency-sensitive systems. Those are open questions a reader should test against their own workload rather than assume from the documentation.
sections.heading: Limits and open questions
